_meta.descricao: Broad periods in the history of the Church, presented as a didactic framework.
_meta.aviso: The division into periods is a didactic device, not an official classification of the Church; the century boundaries are approximate and debated among historians.
_meta.revisao_editorial: Each period cites only facts with widely documented dates (councils, edicts, papal documents). No date has been rounded to give an impression of precision, and the transitions between periods are explicitly shown as approximate.

itens.resumo: From Pentecost to the legal recognition of Christianity in the Roman Empire: the apostolic age, the Fathers of the Church, and the persecutions.
itens.corpo:
The period begins with Pentecost and the preaching of the Apostles, narrated in the Acts of the Apostles, and extends through the first centuries of Christianity's expansion across the Mediterranean basin, up to the Constantinian turn of the early fourth century.

In the so-called apostolic age, the Christian message spread from Jerusalem to Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth, Rome, and other cities of the Empire, above all through the missionary work of Paul of Tarsus, whose letters to the communities he founded are the oldest Christian texts to have come down to us. Tradition places the martyrdom of Peter and Paul in Rome, under Nero, around the year 64-67 — Peter crucified upside down, because he did not consider himself worthy to die as the Master did, Paul beheaded because he was a Roman citizen.

After the death of the last generation of apostles, the transmission of the faith passed to the so-called Apostolic Fathers, direct or indirect disciples of the Twelve: Clement of Rome, whose letter to the Corinthians (c. 96) is one of the earliest Christian documents outside the New Testament; Ignatius of Antioch, who wrote letters to the churches while being taken to Rome for martyrdom, around 107-110, and in them already bears witness to a structure of bishop, presbyters, and deacons in each community; and Polycarp of Smyrna, martyred in old age in the mid-second century. They were followed by the apologists — Justin Martyr is the best known — who sought to explain and defend the Christian faith before Greco-Roman culture and against the accusations of atheism, ritual cannibalism, and immorality that circulated against Christians.

The Roman persecutions were not a continuous phenomenon, but a series of localized and intermittent episodes, which worsened at specific moments: under Nero, after the burning of Rome in 64; under Domitian, at the end of the first century; and, more systematically and on an imperial scale, under Decius, in 250, who required all subjects to offer a public sacrifice to the gods of the State, and under Diocletian, between 303 and 311, in the so-called Great Persecution, the most violent and extensive of all. In these episodes there died figures such as Bishop Cyprian of Carthage (258) and the young Perpetua, executed in Carthage with her slave Felicity (203), whose account of martyrdom is one of the most widely read in ancient Christian literature. The memory of the martyrs — preserved in acts, local calendars, and in the veneration at their tombs — became foundational to ancient Christian spirituality, giving rise to the veneration of relics and to the practice of celebrating the Eucharist over the graves of martyrs, a foreshadowing of the future consecration of altars.

Meanwhile, the Church was consolidating its internal organization. The monarchical episcopate — a single bishop at the head of each local community, surrounded by presbyters and deacons — became widespread over the course of the second century. The canon of the New Testament took shape progressively, in a process that would take centuries to reach its definitive fixation, and the first fixed forms of baptismal and Eucharistic liturgy developed, described for example in the «Didache» and in Justin's «First Apology». The first great internal doctrinal controversies also arose, such as Gnosticism — which denied the goodness of material creation and saw in Christ only the appearance of a human body — and the struggle waged against it by authors such as Irenaeus of Lyon.

The Edict of Milan, an agreement reached in 313 between the emperors Constantine and Licinius, radically changed the legal situation of Christians in the Empire, granting them freedom of worship and ordering the restitution of confiscated property. Constantine's personal conversion, although gradual and theologically ambiguous until his deathbed baptism (337), opened the way for a new kind of relationship between the Church and political power. A few years later, in 325, Constantine himself convened and presided over the opening of the Council of Nicaea, the first ecumenical council, gathered to respond to the Arian controversy over the divinity of the Son. These two milestones — the end of legal persecution and the beginning of the era of the great councils — are used here as an approximate boundary between the early Church and the Middle Ages that would follow, although Christianity would only become the official religion of the Empire under Theodosius, through the Edict of Thessalonica of 380.

itens.resumo: Monasticism, the Christianization of Europe, universities and Scholasticism; also the schism between East and West.
itens.corpo:
Conventionally placed between the 5th and 15th centuries — from the fall of the Western Roman Empire (476) to the capture of Constantinople by the Ottoman Turks (1453) or the European arrival in the Americas (1492) —, the Middle Ages is the period in which the Church took a decisive part in the formation of European civilization, largely filling the vacuum of authority left by the collapse of the Roman administrative structures in the West.

Monasticism was one of the great cultural engines of this age. The Rule of Saint Benedict of Nursia, written in the 6th century and organized around the motto "ora et labora", became the reference for Western monastic life, and the Benedictine monasteries — later also Cluniac and Cistercian ones — functioned as centers of prayer, but also of agriculture, of the copying and preservation of ancient manuscripts, and of literacy, in a period when formal instruction was rare outside them. The so-called Carolingian Renaissance, promoted by Charlemagne from the 8th century onward, relied directly on monastic and cathedral schools to recover the teaching of Latin and of the classical texts.

In the 13th century the mendicant orders appeared — the Franciscans, founded by Francis of Assisi, and the Dominicans, founded by Dominic de Guzmán —, which broke with the model of the fixed, property-owning monastery in order to live on alms and preach in the rapidly expanding cities, responding to a context of growing urbanization and to the emergence of heterodox movements such as Catharism. It is also the century in which the first universities were born — Bologna, Paris, Oxford — out of cathedral schools that obtained their own statutes as corporations of masters and students, with curricula that included the liberal arts, law, medicine and theology.

From this university environment Scholasticism was born, a method of inquiry that sought to harmonize revealed faith with philosophical reason, above all in light of the work of Aristotle, rediscovered in the West largely through Arabic translations and contact with the Islamic world of Iberia. Its greatest exponent was Saint Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican who taught in Paris and Naples and whose "Summa Theologiae", left unfinished at his death in 1274, became an enduring reference of Catholic theology; before him, Anselm of Canterbury and Peter Abelard, among others, had already explored the limits and possibilities of this dialogue between faith and reason. The same period consolidated canon law as a systematic discipline, above all from the "Decretum of Gratian" (c. 1140), and saw Gothic art flourish in the great cathedrals — Chartres, Notre-Dame de Paris, Cologne — conceived as true theological syntheses in stone and stained glass.

The Middle Ages was also a time of serious tensions and crises within the Church itself and in its relations with temporal power. The rupture between Greek-speaking Eastern Christianity and Latin-speaking Western Christianity, which had been deepening for centuries because of liturgical and disciplinary differences and over the authority of the papacy, had in 1054 — when delegates of Pope Leo IX and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchanged mutual excommunications — its traditional landmark, although the actual separation of the two traditions was a gradual process, aggravated still further by the Christian sack of Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade (1204). On the political level, the Investiture Controversy, between the reforming papacy and the Holy Roman Empire, pitted spiritual authority against temporal authority for decades over the appointment of bishops, with its most dramatic episode at Canossa (1077); similar disputes would also mark the conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip IV of France in the early 14th century.

The medieval councils are a central part of this history: from Lateran I (1123), the first ecumenical council of the Latin West, to the Council of Constance (1414-1418), which ended the Western Schism, by way of Lateran IV (1215), which defined Eucharistic transubstantiation, and the troubled period of the Avignon papacy (1309-1377) and of the Schism itself, in which there came to be as many as three rival popes at the same time. The Middle Ages ends, for the purposes of this didactic framing, when the pressures — humanist, political and religious — begin to accumulate that would lead to the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century.

itens.resumo: The Protestant Reformation, the Council of Trent and the Catholic reform, missionary expansion and new congregations.
itens.corpo:
Beginning in 1517, when Martin Luther made public his criticism of the preaching of indulgences, the Protestant Reformation broke the religious unity of Western Europe within a few decades, giving rise to Lutheranism, Calvinism, Anglicanism (1534) and many smaller movements. The doctrinal and disciplinary response of the Catholic Church was articulated above all at the Council of Trent, convoked by Paul III and concluded by Pius IV over twenty-five sessions between 1545 and 1563: the council reaffirmed Scripture and Tradition as joint sources of Revelation, defined the doctrine on original sin, justification and the seven sacraments, and established measures for the deep reform of clerical life, such as the obligatory founding of seminaries and the residence of bishops in their dioceses. From this effort were born, in the following decades, the Roman Catechism (1566), the Roman Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570), which unified the Latin liturgy for four centuries.

The same period saw the birth or consolidation of congregations and orders with a strong impulse toward mission, education and spiritual renewal. The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved by Pope Paul III in 1540, became the most visible instrument of the so-called Counter-Reformation, with colleges spread across Catholic Europe and missions that took Jesuits such as Francis Xavier to India and Japan, and others to China, Africa and the Americas. At the same time, Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross reformed the Carmelite order and left, in the Spanish mystical tradition of the sixteenth century, one of the most elaborate expressions of Christian contemplative life; Philip Neri founded the Oratory in Rome, and Charles Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, became a model of the practical application of the Tridentine reforms in diocesan life.

The missionary expansion tied to European navigation — beginning with the Iberian voyages started in the fifteenth century — carried evangelization to the Americas, Africa and Asia, under the system of the Padroado (patronage), which bound missionary activity to the interests of the crowns of Portugal and Spain. The period produced both lasting fruits, such as the Jesuit reductions in South America and the inculturation attempted by missionaries such as Matteo Ricci in China, and episodes of violence, cultural imposition and complicity with colonial and slaveholding structures, denounced already at the time by voices such as that of the Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas.

The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries brought new doctrinal and political challenges: the controversies surrounding Jansenism and Quietism, the regalism of the Catholic monarchies — which claimed greater control over the Church in their territories — and, on the intellectual plane, the rise of the Enlightenment, which directly challenged traditional religious authority. Under pressure from the Iberian crowns and France, Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773, a decision reversed only in 1814 by Pius VII. The French Revolution (1789-1799) radicalized this confrontation, with the nationalization of ecclesiastical property, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the direct persecution of the refractory clergy, culminating in the imprisonment of Pope Pius VI, who died in captivity in 1799.

The nineteenth century, marked by the Napoleonic wars and the subsequent restoration, saw the Church definitively lose its temporal power with the occupation of Rome by the Kingdom of Italy in 1870, which put an end to the Papal States. In that same year, interrupted by the invasion of the city, the First Vatican Council — convoked by Pius IX and assembled from December 1869 — defined the dogma of papal infallibility in the constitution «Pastor Aeternus» and the relationship between faith and reason in the constitution «Dei Filius». These events symbolically close the modern era and open the way to the challenges of the contemporary era: the social question, the world wars and, in the twentieth century, the Second Vatican Council itself.

itens.titulo: The Origin of the Fish Symbol (Ichthys)
itens.resumo: How a Greek acrostic became one of the oldest signs of recognition among Christians persecuted by the Roman Empire.
itens.corpo:
In the first centuries of Christianity, under constant risk of denunciation and persecution, Christians turned to discreet symbols, ambiguous to the eyes of those who did not share the faith, in order to recognize one another in public without exposing themselves to the Roman authorities. Among these signs — alongside the anchor, which evoked Christian hope disguised as an ordinary nautical object, and the figure of the Good Shepherd — the most enduring was the fish, linked to the Greek acrostic «ichthys» (Ἰχθύς, «fish»): each of the five Greek letters begins a word of a condensed profession of faith — Iesous CHristos THeou Yios Soter, that is, «Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior». It was not an acronym deliberately created for this purpose, but a play between the common Greek word for "fish" and a phrase of faith that fit exactly into its letters — a mnemonic and catechetical device that also served as a password.

Tradition, although difficult to verify documentarily, describes a practical use of the symbol as a code of mutual recognition: a Christian would draw on the ground, in an unassuming way, a simple arc resembling half of a fish; if the other person completed the drawing with the symmetrical arc, he confirmed that he belonged to the same community of faith, without a single word needing to be exchanged in front of strangers. This kind of sign made sense in a context in which gathering openly as a Christian could mean denunciation, imprisonment, or death, especially during the more systematic waves of persecution, such as those promoted by the emperors Decius, in 250, and Diocletian, between 303 and 311.

The symbol also resonates with several Gospel passages that gave the fish a theological meaning broader than that of a mere secret code: the multiplication of the loaves and fish narrated in all four Gospels, Jesus' call to the first disciples — fishermen by trade on the Sea of Galilee — to become «fishers of men» (Mt 4:19), and the several post-Paschal meals in which the Risen One shares fish with the apostles (Jn 21). Through these connections, the ichthys was not merely a password for survival, but also a visual summary of the Christian's baptismal and Eucharistic identity.

Archaeologically, the symbol appears frequently in funerary inscriptions, frescoes, and everyday objects from Christian sites of the 2nd and 3rd centuries — in the catacombs of Rome, such as those of Saint Callixtus and Priscilla, where early Christian epitaphs combine the fish with anchors and the monogram of Christ, and in cities of Asia Minor, such as Ephesus, where an inscription carved in stone near the ancient theater of the city is today one of the most photographed testimonies of the symbol. In some of these finds, the ichthys appears associated with the so-called "monogram of Christ" (the Chi-Rho), reinforcing its function as a discreet sign of Christian identification in a predominantly pagan public space.

With the legalization of Christianity by the Edict of Milan, in 313, and its later adoption as the religion of the Empire under Theodosius, in 380, the need for discreet symbols of recognition lost its meaning: the cross, which previously referred directly to the Roman punishment reserved for slaves and criminals, was able to emerge as the public and central symbol of the Christian faith, and the use of the fish as a sign of identification practically disappeared from the daily life of the Church throughout the Middle Ages, surviving mainly in artistic and learned symbolic contexts.

The symbol was rediscovered and popularized from the second half of the 20th century, when Christian communities — above all evangelical ones in the United States, but Catholic ones as well — once again adopted the stylized design of two arcs as a car sticker, piece of jewelry, or logo, consciously reclaiming its ancient meaning as a public and at the same time discreet affirmation of Christian identity. Today the ichthys is one of the most recognizable Christian symbols in the whole world, present in contexts ranging from personal devotion to cultural debate about religious symbols in the public space, in a course that completely reversed its original function: from a secret sign of survival to an open symbol of belonging.

itens.titulo: The Great Schism of the East (1054)
itens.resumo: A rupture of communion between the Church of Rome and the Churches of the Byzantine East, rooted in theological, liturgical, and jurisdictional differences.
itens.corpo:
In July 1054, Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, head of a legation sent to Constantinople by Pope Leo IX (who had died shortly before, while the mission was still under way), laid upon the altar of the Basilica of Hagia Sophia a bull of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius. Days later, a synod convened by Cerularius himself responded by excommunicating the Roman legates. This specific episode — technically limited to a few individuals, not to the two Churches as a whole — became symbolically associated with the beginning of the so-called Great Schism of the East: the rupture of full communion between the Latin Church, centered on Rome, and the Greek-speaking Byzantine Churches, which came to form what is known today as Orthodoxy.

The causes of the rupture were earlier and far deeper than the episode of 1054, which functioned more as a trigger than as the real origin of the schism. Since the ninth century there had already been serious tensions between Rome and Constantinople, such as the so-called Photian Schism (867-870/879-880), motivated by disputes over ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the Balkans and over the legitimacy of successive patriarchs. Among the underlying causes, the controversy over the «Filioque» stands out: the original Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed stated that the Holy Spirit «proceeds from the Father», and the Latin Church, from the sixth to the eleventh century, came to add unilaterally the phrase «and the Son» (Filioque) — a theological clarification that, for the East, violated both the literal integrity of a creed fixed by an ecumenical council and the principle that changes to the common faith would require conciliar consensus, not the unilateral decision of a single see.

To the theological questions were added liturgical and disciplinary differences that, although they seem secondary today, carried great symbolic weight at the time: the use of unleavened bread (azymes) in the Latin Eucharist, as opposed to the leavened bread of the Byzantine tradition; the mandatory celibacy of the Latin clergy, different from the Eastern practice that permits the marriage of priests (but not of bishops); differences in fasting, in the liturgical calendar, and in points of canonical discipline. Behind all this lay the underlying and most irreducible question: the authority and primacy of the bishop of Rome. While Rome upheld a primacy of universal jurisdiction, founded on the succession of Peter, Constantinople recognized in the pope only a primacy of honor among equals — «primus inter pares» — without power of direct intervention over the other patriarchal sees of the East.

The political and cultural context also contributed decisively to the estrangement: the progressive division of the former Roman Empire into a Latin western half, Christianized under the influence of Rome and later of the Germanic kingdoms and the Holy Roman Empire, and a Greek eastern half, centered on Constantinople, which saw itself as the direct continuation of the Roman Empire. The coronation of Charlemagne as emperor of the West by Pope Leo III in 800 had already been received in Constantinople as a usurpation, deepening the mutual distrust between the two Christendoms, which had been drifting apart culturally and linguistically for centuries.

After 1054, the rupture was not immediately felt in its full extent by ordinary faithful, and for decades relations between Rome and Constantinople continued to exist, though tense. The episode that made the schism irreversible in the popular perception came much later: the Christian sack of Constantinople by the crusaders of the Fourth Crusade in 1204, when Western armies, diverted from their original destination in the Holy Land, plundered the Byzantine capital, desecrated churches, and installed a Latin Empire of the East for decades — a trauma that Orthodox memory preserves to this day as the greatest symbol of Latin hostility.

The mutual excommunications of 1054 remained formally in force for more than nine hundred years, until they were solemnly lifted on December 7, 1965, on the eve of the closing of the Second Vatican Council, in a simultaneous gesture by Pope Paul VI in Rome and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I in Constantinople, by means of a Common Declaration signed by both. The gesture, the fruit of the historic meeting between the two leaders in Jerusalem in 1964, did not restore full ecclesial communion between the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Churches — which continue to differ on the papal primacy and other questions — but it opened a theological dialogue and a fraternal relationship that has continued through the following pontificates, including meetings between Popes Francis and Benedict XVI and the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I.

itens.resumo: The arrival of Christianity on the American continent from the end of the fifteenth century, between missionary action and the tensions of colonization.
itens.corpo:
The evangelization of Latin America began with the arrival of Spanish and Portuguese navigators and colonizers on the continent from 1492, under the regime of the royal patronage (padroado), by which the papacy delegated to the Iberian crowns broad powers over the ecclesiastical organization of their overseas territories in exchange for the commitment to sustain and promote the mission. Religious accompanied the very first expeditions: Franciscans and Dominicans arrived among the first colonizers in the Caribbean and Mexico, followed by Augustinians and Mercedarians, and from the middle of the sixteenth century by the Society of Jesus, founded in 1540 and quickly launched into missionary work across practically the entire continent.

These orders organized an extensive system of doctrinas, convents, colleges and reductions to catechize the indigenous peoples — often learning and systematizing their languages in grammars and bilingual catechisms, a linguistic and ethnographic work of great historical value. The best-known example of this missionary model is the Jesuit-Guaraní reductions, begun in 1610 in the region that today corresponds to the border between Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay — the Reduction of São Nicolau, founded in 1626 by Father Roque González de Santa Cruz on the banks of the Uruguay River, was one of the first in what is now the territory of Rio Grande do Sul. In these communities, tens of thousands of Guaranis lived under their own social, productive and religious organization, relatively protected from direct enslavement by settlers and bandeirantes, in a model that current historiography discusses both as an experience of protection and as a form of cultural tutelage.

The period was marked by deep tensions between the evangelizing mission and the logic of conquest and colonization. Alongside missionaries who publicly denounced the abuses committed against the indigenous peoples — the best-known case being that of the Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas (1484-1566), who after years as a colonist on the island of Hispaniola became a friar and devoted the rest of his life to defending the rights of the indigenous before the Spanish Crown, documenting mistreatment and mass deaths in works such as the «A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies» (1552) —, there was also systematic violence, forced cultural imposition, destruction of codices and native religious traditions, and the complicity of a considerable part of the colonial clergy with the encomienda system and, later, with the enslavement of Africans brought to the continent. The historical assessment of this period remains a subject of academic and ecclesial debate, acknowledged even by recent popes: John Paul II asked forgiveness for the sins committed in the evangelization of the Americas, and Pope Francis himself, during a trip to Bolivia in 2015, humbly asked forgiveness for the «grave sins» committed against the indigenous peoples during the so-called conquest of America.

Missionary action was not limited to Spanish America: in Portuguese Brazil, Jesuits such as Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta arrived as early as 1549 with the first governor-general, Tomé de Sousa, founding the first colleges and indigenous settlements (aldeamentos) in Bahia and later in São Paulo, and developing, as in Spanish America, an extensive production of grammars and catechisms in indigenous languages, above all Tupi.

From this evangelization, marked by so many contradictions, there also arose popular devotions that would become central to Latin American Catholic identity and would survive all later political changes. The oldest and most influential is Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose apparition to the indigenous man Juan Diego, on the hill of Tepeyac, near Mexico City, is traditionally dated to December 1531 — a devotion that combined elements of European Marian devotion with an iconography and a narrative deeply rooted in indigenous experience, becoming patroness of the entire American continent. In Brazil, the devotion to Our Lady of Aparecida was born from the finding of a terracotta image by fishermen in the Paraíba do Sul River in 1717, and would grow over the following centuries until it became, in the twentieth century, the national patroness of the country.

The centuries of evangelization produced, in the end, the most visible demographic result of this process: Latin America today has the largest Catholic population in the world, even though, since the last decades of the twentieth century, it has faced rapid growth of Pentecostal evangelical churches and of the unbelieving, which is significantly reshaping the religious map of the continent.

itens.resumo: Agreement between the emperors Constantine and Licinius that granted religious toleration to Christianity, ending centuries of legal persecution in Rome.
itens.corpo:
In the winter of 312 to 313, two emperors shared power over a Roman Empire that was still formally tetrarchic: Constantine, lord of the West since his victory over Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in October 312 — a victory that Christian tradition, above all through Eusebius of Caesarea and Lactantius, associates with a vision or dream in which Constantine is said to have received the sign of Christ before the battle —, and Licinius, lord of the East. In February 313, the two met in Milan to seal a political alliance, reinforced by Licinius's marriage to Constantia, Constantine's half-sister, and took advantage of the meeting to settle a common policy toward the Christians, whose legal situation stemmed from decades of intermittent persecutions, the most recent and violent of which had been the Great Persecution begun by Diocletian in 303.

What became known in school and popular tradition as the "Edict of Milan" was not, technically, an edict drawn up and promulgated in the city itself. What existed, according to the current historiographical consensus, was an agreement of principles concluded in Milan between the two emperors, subsequently communicated to the provinces of the Empire by means of letters and instructions to the governors — the best known of these is the letter addressed to the governor of Bithynia, preserved by Lactantius in «On the Deaths of the Persecutors» and by Eusebius of Caesarea in his «Ecclesiastical History», the only two ancient sources that preserve the essentials of the text. Modern historians also debate to what extent the agreement of 313 represented a real novelty, since the emperor Galerius, Licinius's predecessor in the East, had already published in 311, shortly before his death, a first edict of toleration that suspended the persecution — the «Agreement of Milan» would thus have confirmed, broadened and standardized this toleration throughout the Empire, rather than creating it from scratch.

In its content, the text established freedom of worship for Christians and for all the other subjects of the Empire, «so that each one may give his soul's assent to the religion he judges most suitable» — a formulation of general religious toleration, and not a measure exclusive to Christianity, although Christianity was its most evident and intended beneficiary. The agreement also ordered the restitution to Christians, without compensation from the State, of the places of worship and other property that had been confiscated from them during the earlier persecutions, including properties that had already been resold or given to third parties.

The practical consequences were profound and rapid. Christians ceased to live in hiding or under constant threat of denunciation, and the Church was able to organize itself publicly again, build visible places of worship and recover its patrimony. Constantine went beyond mere toleration: he actively favored the Church with donations, tax exemptions for the clergy and the construction of great basilicas in Rome, such as that of Saint John Lateran and the original Basilica of Saint Peter. A little over a decade later, in 325, Constantine himself would convene and preside over the opening of the Council of Nicaea, a sign of the new role that emperors would come to play in the internal affairs of the Church.

It is important to note that the toleration of 313 was not yet equivalent to making Christianity the official religion of the State: Roman paganism continued to be practiced freely, and other fourth-century emperors, such as Julian the Apostate, would even attempt to partially reverse the Christian ascendancy. The next decisive step, the proclamation of Nicene Christianity as the official religion of the whole Roman Empire, with the consequent gradual loss of legal status of pagan worship, would come only decades later, on 27 February 380, through the Edict of Thessalonica, promulgated by the emperor Theodosius I jointly with Gratian and Valentinian II.

itens.resumo: A gathering convened by Emperor Constantine that defined the full divinity of the Son against Arianism, and set the common date of Easter.
itens.corpo:
Convened by Emperor Constantine, newly victorious over Licinius and now sole master of a reunified Empire, the Council of Nicaea met in the summer of 325 in the Bithynian city that gives it its name, near the new capital that Constantine was planning on the Bosphorus. It was the first time in history that bishops from all over the Empire — about three hundred, according to the most widely accepted estimates, although later tradition rounded the number to 318 by symbolic association with the number of Abraham's servants in the Book of Genesis — gathered in a single assembly, funded and organized by the imperial power itself, which provided transportation and lodging for the participants. Most of the bishops came from the Greek-speaking East — Asia Minor, Syria, Palestine, Egypt — and only a handful represented the Latin West; Pope Saint Sylvester I, already elderly, did not attend in person, sending two legates.

The immediate reason for the convocation was the controversy stirred up by Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who taught that the Son, though superior to all creation, was himself created by the Father out of nothing, and therefore was neither eternal nor of the same divine substance — "there was a time when he was not," in the formula that became his trademark. The dispute was already seriously dividing the Christian communities of Egypt and the East when Constantine, more concerned with the political and social unity of the Empire than with theological subtleties, decided to call a general council to settle it once and for all, after a first failed attempt at reconciliation by means of a letter sent to Alexandria by Bishop Hosius of Córdoba, his trusted ecclesiastical adviser.

After intense debates, the overwhelming majority of the bishops present — only two, besides Arius himself, refused to sign — subscribed to a creed that defined the Son as "begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" (in Greek, homoousios, "of the same substance"), a term that did not appear in Scripture but which the conciliar fathers judged necessary to definitively close the interpretive gaps that biblical language, by itself, left open to Arianism. The Creed of Nicaea was later expanded and reformulated at the Council of Constantinople I, in 381, especially with regard to the Holy Spirit, giving rise to the text now known as the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, still professed today in Catholic and Orthodox liturgies and in those of various Protestant denominations.

Beyond the central Christological question, the council set about fixing a common date for the celebration of Easter, which until then had been celebrated on different days depending on the region — some Eastern communities tied it directly to the date of the Jewish Passover calendar (14 Nisan), a practice known as Quartodecimanism, while Rome and Alexandria already always celebrated on a Sunday. The council decided that Christian Easter should always be celebrated on a Sunday, and delegated to the Church of Alexandria, recognized for its astronomical tradition, the yearly calculation of the exact date based on the first full moon after the spring equinox — a system of calculation, with later adjustments, that remains in use today. The council also promulgated twenty disciplinary canons, dealing with questions such as the hierarchy among the great episcopal sees (Rome, Alexandria, Antioch), the minimum age for ordination, and the reconciliation of repentant schismatics and heretics with the Church.

The consequences of the condemnation of Arianism at Nicaea were neither immediate nor definitive: in the following decades, under the protection of various emperors sympathetic to the Arian cause, among them Constantius II, Constantine's own son, Arianism remained influential for a good part of the fourth century, and was also carried by missionaries such as Ulfilas to the Germanic peoples, among whom it would remain dominant for centuries, even after its definitive condemnation within the Empire by the Council of Constantinople I. Despite this long survival, Nicaea I is considered the first of the twenty-one councils recognized as ecumenical by the Catholic Church, and its Christological formula remains, almost seventeen centuries later, the core of the Trinitarian profession of faith held by practically all the great Christian traditions.

itens.resumo: A dispute between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire in the eleventh century over who had the authority to appoint bishops and abbots.
itens.corpo:
Throughout the eleventh century, a movement of internal reform of the Church — today called the Gregorian Reform, after its chief promoter, Pope Gregory VII (1073-1085) — sought to combat two evils that the ecclesiastical hierarchy considered deeply rooted: simony, that is, the buying and selling of offices and sacraments, and Nicolaitism, the concubinage and marriage of clerics, which the reform saw as incompatible with the purity of priestly ministry. At the center of this reform was a fundamental institutional question: who truly held the authority to appoint and invest bishops and abbots — the papacy, by spiritual right, or the kings and emperors, who had for centuries exercised this power in practice, attaching to ecclesiastical offices extensive fiefs and territorial revenues.

Before Gregory VII, it was a common and widely accepted practice for kings and emperors to personally choose and invest bishops and abbots with the symbols of their office — the ring and the pastoral staff — while handing over to them control of ecclesiastical lands and revenues that made these prelates, in practice, vassals of the secular power. Gregory VII saw in this practice a contamination of the freedom of the Church (the so-called "libertas Ecclesiae") by temporal power, and in 1075, in the so-called "Dictatus Papae," he categorically asserted the supremacy of papal authority over all Christendom, including the power to depose emperors.

The conflict with Emperor Henry IV of the Holy Roman Empire broke out when he, defying the new Gregorian norms, continued to appoint bishops in Italy and Germany on his own. Gregory VII threatened to excommunicate him; Henry responded by convening a synod of German bishops at Worms in January 1076, which declared Gregory deposed from the papacy. The pope reacted by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oath of fidelity — a political weapon that proved devastating, since the German princes, already discontented with the emperor, threatened to elect a successor if he did not obtain papal forgiveness within a year.

The most dramatic and symbolic episode of this confrontation took place in the winter of 1077: Henry IV, to avoid deposition, crossed the Alps in the dead of winter and presented himself as a penitent before the castle of Canossa, in Tuscany, where Gregory VII was staying under the protection of Countess Matilda of Canossa. According to the traditional account, Henry remained for three days barefoot and dressed as a penitent before the castle, in the snow, until the pope agreed to lift the excommunication — a gesture of public humiliation that became, in Western culture, a byword for forced submission ("to go to Canossa"). The reconciliation, however, was merely tactical: a few years later the conflict flared up again, the German princes elected a rival anti-king, and Henry eventually marched on Rome in 1084, forcing Gregory VII into exile in Salerno, where he would die in 1085.

The conflict, with varying intensity, continued under the successors of both for more than four decades, also involving similar disputes in England (between King Henry I and Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury) and in France. The definitive solution for the German case came only with the Concordat of Worms, signed on September 23, 1122, between Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V, son and successor of Henry IV. The agreement clearly distinguished two spheres that until then had been confused: the spiritual investiture of the office — symbolized by the ring and the staff — became the exclusive prerogative of the Church, carried out through free canonical election by the local clergy; the temporal investiture — symbolized by the scepter, and concerning the fiefs and territorial revenues attached to the office — remained a prerogative of the emperor, but only after the ecclesiastical election.

The Concordat of Worms was solemnly ratified the following year by the First Lateran Council (1123), recognized as the first ecumenical council presided over entirely by a pope without imperial convocation — a symbolic sign that, although the final compromise was a middle-ground solution and not a total victory for the papacy, the Investiture Controversy left as a lasting legacy the principle that the appointment of bishops is, in its essence, a spiritual act that belongs to the Church and not to political power — a principle that would shape, from then on, the entire relationship between the Holy See and the European states.

itens.resumo: A series of military expeditions between the 11th and 13th centuries, called to aid the Byzantine Empire and to retake the Holy Land from Muslim rule.
itens.corpo:
In November 1095, Pope Urban II closed the Council of Clermont, in France, with a sermon that would become one of the most consequential speeches of medieval history: responding to a request for military aid from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, threatened by the advance of the Seljuk Turks in Asia Minor, Urban exhorted the Christian knighthood of western Europe to stop their wars against one another and to take up arms to aid the Eastern Christians and free Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre from Muslim rule — the city had been under Islamic control since the seventh century, and access for Christian pilgrims had become more difficult under the new Seljuk rule. As a spiritual incentive, the pope promised a plenary indulgence, the remission of all temporal punishment due to sins, to those who took part in the expedition out of motives of faith.

The popular response far exceeded expectations: alongside the noble armies that set out in an orderly fashion under leaders such as Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto, and Raymond of Toulouse, a spontaneous and poorly armed wave of peasants and poor people also formed, known as the People's Crusade or the Peasants' Crusade, led by the preacher Peter the Hermit, which set out before the regular armies and was virtually wiped out by the Turks in Anatolia. The First Crusade, the most successful of all the expeditions, conquered Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, after a brutal siege that ended in a general massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish population — an episode of violence that later Christian historiography itself would recognize as deeply contradictory to the Gospel ideal that supposedly motivated the expedition. From the conquest were born four Latin Crusader States in the East: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Tripoli, the Principality of Antioch, and the County of Edessa.

In the following decades, as the Muslim powers reorganized under leaders such as Zengi, Nur ad-Din, and above all Saladin — who unified Egypt and Syria under his command — the Crusader States were gradually put under pressure. The fall of Edessa in 1144 prompted the Second Crusade (1147-1149), preached by Bernard of Clairvaux and led by Kings Louis VII of France and Conrad III of the Holy Roman Empire, which failed without lasting gains. The decisive defeat of the Crusaders came at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, after which Saladin retook Jerusalem almost ninety years after its original conquest, putting an end to the Christian presence in the city. The response was the Third Crusade (1189-1192), which brought together three of the greatest monarchs of Europe — Richard the Lionheart of England, Philip Augustus of France, and the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who drowned on the way to the Holy Land — but which, despite recovering part of the coast, failed to retake Jerusalem, ending with a peace treaty between Richard and Saladin that guaranteed only pilgrims' access to the city.

The most controversial episode of the entire crusading movement occurred in the Fourth Crusade (1202-1204): diverted from its original destination in Egypt by financial and political pressures — above all from the Republic of Venice, which had financed the fleet — and by the dynastic dispute over the Byzantine throne, the expedition ended up sacking Constantinople, capital of the very Christian Byzantine Empire that the crusades had originally set out to aid, in April 1204. The sack, with the plundering of relics, works of art, and treasures of the city and the establishment of a Latin Empire of the East that would last until 1261, is now recognized, including by the Catholic Church, as one of the most shameful episodes and an irreparable blow to relations between Latin and Orthodox Christians — Pope John Paul II formally asked forgiveness for the episode in a letter to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I in 2001.

Altogether, eight great numbered crusades are traditionally counted over almost two centuries, in addition to smaller expeditions, such as the disastrous Children's Crusade (1212) and the late crusades of King Louis IX of France to Egypt and Tunisia in the thirteenth century, in which the king himself would die. The last Crusader stronghold in the East, the city of Acre, fell in 1291, definitively ending the Latin presence in the Holy Land. The historical assessment of the phenomenon of the Crusades is today the subject of critical revision also within the Catholic Church itself, which recognizes in them genuine religious motivations — the sincere desire of many pilgrim-warriors to protect the holy places and the Eastern Christians — alongside the political, economic, and territorial interests of the European powers, and episodes of violence, religious intolerance, and massacres of Jewish, Muslim, and Eastern Christian civilians that depart sharply from the spirit of the Gospel.

itens.resumo: Ecclesiastical tribunals established from the thirteenth century onward to judge heresy, whose historical activity is today the object of critical review by the Church.
itens.corpo:
The word "Inquisition" designates, in fact, not a single, continuous institution, but a succession of distinct tribunals, created in different eras and contexts, with jurisdictions, methods and degrees of severity that varied considerably among them — an essential distinction that popular memory tends to erase by treating the phenomenon as a homogeneous block of a thousand years of persecution.

The first organized form, today called the medieval or papal Inquisition, arose in the context of the struggle against the Cathar (or Albigensian) heresy in the south of France and against the Waldensians, movements that rejected central points of Catholic doctrine and hierarchy and that the Church also saw as a threat to the social and political order of the time. After preliminary measures taken by councils of the twelfth century, it was above all Pope Gregory IX, in 1231-1233, who institutionalized specialized tribunals, entrusted chiefly to Dominican and Franciscan friars — recently founded orders, trained in theology and preaching —, removing the judgment of heresy from the hands of local bishops and secular courts and submitting it to inquisitors appointed directly by Rome. The inquisitorial procedure provided for interrogation, the possibility of retraction and penance for the repentant, and the handing over to the "secular arm" — that is, to the civil authorities, responsible for carrying out the death penalty — only of relapsed or impenitent heretics; torture, authorized by Pope Innocent IV in 1252 under limited conditions, was used with a frequency that varied according to region and tribunal.

The Spanish Inquisition, created in 1478 by the bull "Exigit Sinceras Devotionis Affectus" of Pope Sixtus IV at the request of the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, was an institution of a rather different nature: although formally authorized by Rome, it functioned under almost total control of the Spanish Crown, which appointed the inquisitor general and also used the tribunal as an instrument of political centralization and of control over the populations of Jewish conversos (New Christians) and Moriscos (converted Muslims), suspected of secretly maintaining their previous religious practices. Active until its definitive abolition in 1834, it was responsible for a number of executions that modern historiography, with access to the trial archives, has revised downward from traditional estimates, while still acknowledging a grave toll of persecution, torture and death, especially in its first decades of operation.

The Roman Inquisition, in turn, established in 1542 by Pope Paul III through the constitution "Licet ab Initio" and organized as the Congregation of the Holy Office, arose as a direct response to the advance of the Protestant Reformation in Italy, concentrating its work on combating doctrines considered heretical and on the censorship of books, by means of the famous "Index of Forbidden Books." It was this Roman tribunal — under the direct control of the papacy, and not of the crowns — that prosecuted the best-known cases in the history of modern science, such as those of Giordano Bruno, burned at the stake in 1600 for heterodox theological positions (not strictly for his cosmological ideas), and of Galileo Galilei, condemned in 1633 for defending heliocentrism, forced to recant publicly and kept under house arrest until his death.

Throughout the twentieth century, the historical and theological assessment of this set of tribunals changed substantially within the Church itself. In 1998, Pope John Paul II commissioned the International Theological Commission to undertake an in-depth study of the "errors of the past," which resulted in the document "Memory and Reconciliation: The Church and the Faults of the Past" (1999), explicitly acknowledging that methods of coercion, intolerance and violence had been used by members of the Church in the name of the faith, in a manner incompatible with the Gospel. On the basis of this work, on March 12, 2000 — the so-called "Day of Pardon," celebrated during the Great Jubilee — John Paul II presided over a penitential liturgy in Saint Peter's Basilica in which he publicly asked forgiveness for historical sins committed by Catholics, explicitly including those committed "in the service of truth" by non-evangelical methods, a direct reference to the Inquisition and similar episodes of religious intolerance. At the same time, the Vatican partially opened its archives on the Holy Office to independent historians, in an effort of historical revision that helped correct both the exaggerations of the so-called anti-Catholic "Black Legend" and the apologetic minimizations of the real suffering caused by these tribunals over the centuries.

itens.resumo: Rupture between the Church of England and Rome in the sixteenth century, triggered by the Pope's refusal to annul the marriage of Henry VIII.
itens.corpo:
The crisis that broke the Church of England away from Rome arose from a dynastic question: married since 1509 to Catherine of Aragon, the widow of his older brother and aunt of the powerful Emperor Charles V, King Henry VIII saw with growing anguish that the marriage had not given him a surviving male heir — only a daughter, Mary. From 1527, convinced that the marriage was invalidated by a biblical impediment (Leviticus 20:21), Henry asked Pope Clement VII to annul the union, a request that dragged on for years without a definitive answer, in part because the Pope, at that point, was under heavy political and even military pressure from Emperor Charles V, Catherine's nephew, whose troops had sacked Rome in 1527.

Tired of the delay and already involved with Anne Boleyn, a lady of his court, Henry opted for a unilateral break. In 1533, the new Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, declared the marriage to Catherine null, allowing the king to marry Anne Boleyn secretly. In response, the Pope excommunicated Henry. The institutional break came in November 1534, when the English Parliament passed the "Act of Supremacy," recognizing Henry VIII and his successors as "the only supreme head on earth of the Church of England," with authority over doctrine, ecclesiastical appointments and discipline — a blow that in practice nationalized the English Church and subordinated the clergy to the Crown, more than an immediate doctrinal rupture, since Henry, until his death, kept a good part of Catholic theology and liturgy, persecuting both Catholics loyal to Rome and Protestants considered radical.

Resistance to the break cost the lives of figures of great prominence: the former chancellor Saint Thomas More, author of "Utopia," and Saint John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, refused to swear acceptance of the Act of Supremacy and were beheaded in 1535, condemned for treason; both would be canonized by the Catholic Church in 1935. The dissolution of the English monasteries, between 1536 and 1541, confiscated vast ecclesiastical properties in favor of the Crown and the nobility, financially consolidating the break and making any quick return to Rome practically irreversible.

After the death of Henry VIII in 1547, the reign of his still-underage son, Edward VI, under regents of strong Protestant inclination, radicalized the English religious reform, introducing Cranmer's "Book of Common Prayer" and a theology increasingly close to continental Protestantism. Edward's premature death in 1553 brought to the throne Mary I, the Catholic daughter of Catherine of Aragon, who restored communion with Rome by decree and harshly persecuted Protestants — more than three hundred were burned as heretics during her reign, which earned her the historical nickname "Bloody Mary." This Catholic return, however, was brief: with Mary's death in 1558 and the accession of her half-sister Elizabeth I, daughter of Anne Boleyn, Parliament reestablished the Act of Supremacy in 1559, definitively consolidating the separation of the Church of England from Rome.

From then on, the Church of England developed its own identity, Anglicanism, which sought a middle path ("via media") between Roman Catholicism and continental Protestantism, preserving the episcopal structure and a good part of the traditional liturgy while adopting Reformed theological elements. British colonial expansion would carry Anglicanism throughout the world in the following centuries, giving rise to the present-day Anglican Communion, a federation of autonomous national churches — among them the Episcopal Church in the United States — which recognizes the Archbishop of Canterbury as a symbolic point of reference for unity, without the central jurisdictional authority that characterizes the Catholic papacy.

itens.resumo: Ecumenical council of the sixteenth century that responded doctrinally and disciplinarily to the Protestant Reformation, over nearly twenty years and three pontificates.
itens.corpo:
When Pope Paul III convened the general council that would meet in Trent, a city in northern Italy then part of the Holy Roman Empire, Western Christianity had already lived through more than two decades of rupture since the publication of Martin Luther's 95 Theses in 1517. Several earlier attempts to resolve the crisis by means of imperial diets and theological colloquies — such as the Diet of Worms (1521) and the Colloquy of Regensburg (1541) — had failed, and the religious fragmentation of central Europe was already a fait accompli when the first council fathers finally gathered in Trent in December 1545, after years of postponements caused by political disputes between the pope and Emperor Charles V over where and when the council should take place.

The Council of Trent is distinguished from almost all earlier councils by its extraordinary duration: nearly eighteen years, between 1545 and 1563, divided into three distinct periods of sessions, under three successive popes — Paul III, Julius III and Pius IV —, interrupted by outbreaks of plague, wars in central Europe and changes of location (some of the sessions took place in Bologna). Over that time, several hundred bishops took part in all, although the number present at any specific session varied enormously, being generally smaller in the early phases and growing in the final sessions of 1562-1563.

Doctrinally, Trent responded point by point to the central theses of the Protestant Reformation: against the Lutheran thesis that Scripture alone (sola Scriptura) would suffice as the source of faith, the council affirmed Scripture and apostolic Tradition as joint and inseparable sources of Revelation; against justification by faith alone (sola fide), it defined that justification involves the person's free cooperation with grace; and it reaffirmed the existence and the number of the seven sacraments, which were contested by various Reformed currents that recognized only baptism and the Eucharist. The decree on the Eucharist, of 1551, established the term "transubstantiation" as the official description of the conversion of the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ.

As important as the doctrinal response was the extensive disciplinary reform that the council promoted, responding to internal abuses that the Church itself acknowledged as real and that had fed part of the discontent that gave rise to the Reformation: the obligation of bishops to reside in their dioceses, from which they had until then frequently been absent; the prohibition of the accumulation of multiple ecclesiastical benefices by a single person; and, perhaps the most lasting measure of all, the determination that each diocese establish its own seminary for the formation of future priests, systematically raising the theological, moral and pastoral level of the clergy — a model of priestly formation that, with adaptations, remains in force to this day.

From the Tridentine work there derived, in the years following the close of the council, publications that unified Catholic life for centuries: the Roman Catechism (1566), the Roman Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570), which fixed the so-called "Tridentine Mass", celebrated without major changes until the liturgical reform of the Second Vatican Council, four centuries later. For all these reasons, Trent is considered the founding landmark of the Catholic Counter-Reformation — or, in the terminology preferred by many contemporary historians, of the Catholic Reform —, the movement of internal renewal that restored doctrinal cohesion and disciplinary vigor to the Church at a moment of acute fragmentation, preparing the ground for the missionary and spiritual impetus that would characterize the following centuries.

itens.titulo: The Suppression of the Society of Jesus (1773)
itens.resumo: Temporary dissolution of the Society of Jesus under pressure from the European monarchies, reversed four decades later by Pius VII.
itens.corpo:
The crisis that led to the temporary extinction of the Society of Jesus began decades before 1773, amid the intellectual climate of the Enlightenment and the strengthening of regalism — the doctrine, widespread among the European Catholic monarchies, according to which the State should have broad control over ecclesiastical matters in its territory, including over religious orders directly obedient to Rome. The Jesuits, because of their economic wealth, their educational influence over European elites as confessors and teachers, and their organizational and missionary autonomy — above all in the reductions of South America, where they came to form what was practically a self-governing territory — became a priority target of this movement.

Portugal led the way: in 1759, the prime minister Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, the Marquis of Pombal, expelled the Jesuits from the entire Portuguese empire, accusing them of conspiracy against the Crown after the attempt on the life of King Joseph I in 1758, and of resisting the Crown's interests in the Guarani reductions, which were then disputed between Portugal and Spain under the Treaty of Madrid. Pombal also waged an intense propaganda campaign against the Order throughout Europe, attributing to it a good part of Portugal's educational and economic backwardness. France followed the example between 1762 and 1764, dissolving the Society in its territory after a financial scandal involving a Jesuit in Martinique; the Spain of Charles III expelled the Jesuits from all its dominions, including Spanish America, in 1767, and the Kingdom of Naples did the same in that same year.

With four of the leading Catholic crowns having already expelled the Order from their territories and actively pressing the papacy for total suppression, Pope Clement XIV — elected in 1769 in a conclave in which this pressure weighed heavily on the choice of the new pontiff — yielded after years of resistance and signed, on July 21, 1773, the brief "Dominus ac Redemptor," which suppressed the Society of Jesus throughout the Catholic Church, formally dissolving its collective religious vows, closing its colleges, and confiscating its property, which was generally transferred to other orders or to the State.

The suppression struck a heavy blow to the network of education, missions, and science that the Jesuits had built over more than two centuries: thousands of colleges in Europe, America, and Asia lost their teachers, and entire missions, such as the Guarani reductions, were left without their founders and administrators, accelerating the decline of those communities. Even so, the Order survived, in a manner formally irregular but tolerated by Rome, in two non-Catholic territories whose rulers refused to promulgate the papal brief: Protestant Prussia under Frederick II, who saw in the Jesuits valuable teachers for his educational system, and above all the Russian Empire of Empress Catherine II, where the Orthodox Church was official and the papal decree, therefore, had no automatic legal effect — in these territories, small Jesuit nuclei kept the tradition alive and continued the formation of new members throughout the period of suppression.

The restoration of the Society of Jesus came with the change in the European political situation after the Napoleonic wars: on August 7, 1814, Pope Pius VII, recently returned from the exile imposed by Napoleon, promulgated the bull "Sollicitudo Omnium Ecclesiarum," formally reestablishing the Order throughout the Church, based precisely on the nucleus that had survived in Russia. The reconstituted Society of Jesus would resume, throughout the nineteenth century and beyond, its prominent role in Catholic education and missionary activity, and today it is the largest male religious order of the Catholic Church.

itens.titulo: The Church during the French Revolution
itens.resumo: Religious persecution, confiscation of ecclesiastical property, and an attempt to subordinate the clergy entirely to the State during the French Revolution (1789-1799).
itens.corpo:
In the early years of the French Revolution, the National Constituent Assembly, seeking to resolve the kingdom's grave financial crisis, voted in November 1789 to nationalize all Church property in France — lands, monasteries, ecclesiastical revenues — which came to serve as collateral for the issuance of a new paper currency, the assignats. Although justified by fiscal arguments, the measure struck at the very material sustenance of the French Church and signaled from the start that the Revolution intended not merely to reform the State, but also to profoundly redefine the place of religion in society.

The decisive step came in July 1790, with the approval of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which entirely reorganized the French ecclesiastical structure according to the administrative criteria of the new revolutionary State: the number of dioceses was adjusted to coincide with the new administrative departments, and bishops and pastors came to be elected by assemblies of citizens — including non-Catholics — rather than appointed by the Holy See or by the traditional hierarchy. The law further required all the clergy to take a public oath of fidelity to the kingdom's new Constitution. Pope Pius VI, after nearly a year of deliberation and attempts at negotiation, formally condemned the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in April 1791, by means of the briefs "Quod Aliquantum" and "Caritas," declaring invalid the elections and ordinations made under its rules.

The papal condemnation divided the French clergy into two irreconcilable camps: those who took the oath demanded by the State, called the "juring clergy" or constitutional clergy, and those who refused, remaining faithful to Rome — the "refractory clergy," who quickly became the target of growing political suspicion, being seen by the more radical revolutionaries as agents of a foreign power and of counter-revolutionary resistance. It is estimated that about half of the French clergy refused the oath, a sign of how deep the division that the law had caused within French Catholicism itself was.

With the radicalization of the Revolution from 1792 onward, and especially during the Reign of Terror (1793-1794), under the rule of the Committee of Public Safety led by Robespierre, the persecution of the refractory clergy became systematic and violent: priests were imprisoned, deported to French Guiana in conditions that many did not survive, or summarily executed — the most remembered episode being the September Massacres of 1792, when more than two hundred priests imprisoned in Paris were murdered by mobs within a few days. It is estimated that over the course of the revolutionary period tens of thousands of priests were forced into exile, mainly to England, Italy, and the German states, while hundreds of others were executed or died in prisons and deportations. The most radical phase of the period also saw attempts at the complete dechristianization of French society: churches were closed or turned into "Temples of Reason," the Christian calendar was replaced by a revolutionary calendar without Sundays or saints, and alternative civic cults, such as the "Cult of the Supreme Being" promoted by Robespierre, attempted to replace traditional religious practice.

Pope Pius VI himself would pay with his life for this hostility: already weakened by the loss of the papal territories of northern Italy to the French troops commanded by Napoleon Bonaparte, in 1798 the French general Louis-Alexandre Berthier occupied Rome, proclaimed a short-lived Roman Republic, and demanded that the pope, then eighty years old and gravely ill, renounce temporal power. In the face of his refusal, Pius VI was taken prisoner to France, passing through Siena, Florence, Turin, and Grenoble before being installed in Valence, in the Rhône valley, where he would die on August 29, 1799, still formally a prisoner of the French revolutionary authorities — a dramatic symbol of the lowest point in relations between the Catholic Church and European political power in the modern age. The normalization of these relations would come only years later, with the Concordat of 1801 signed between the Holy See and Napoleon, already under the pontificate of Pius VII.

itens.titulo: The Loss of the Papal States (1870)
itens.resumo: The occupation of Rome by the Kingdom of Italy on September 20, 1870, which ended the temporal power of the popes over a territory of their own until the Lateran Treaties of 1929.
itens.corpo:
The Papal States — a territory that, at the height of its extent, covered a good part of the center of the Italian peninsula, including Rome, Umbria, the Marche, and part of Emilia-Romagna — go back, according to tradition, to the donation of the Frankish king Pepin the Short to Pope Stephen II in 756, and had been governed by the popes as temporal sovereigns, alongside their spiritual authority, for more than a millennium. This dual role of the papacy — spiritual head of the Church and temporal monarch of an Italian state — was considered by many Catholics, over the centuries, a guarantee of the independence of the Holy See from any foreign political power.

This arrangement collapsed definitively with the process of Italian unification (the Risorgimento) throughout the nineteenth century. Between 1860 and 1861, the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, under King Victor Emmanuel II and Prime Minister Camillo Cavour, annexed most of the papal territories — Romagna, Umbria, and the Marche — leaving Pope Pius IX with only Rome and its immediate surroundings (Lazio), until then protected by a French garrison maintained by Emperor Napoleon III in keeping with agreements with the Holy See. When the Franco-Prussian War, begun in July 1870, forced the withdrawal of these French troops for the defense of France itself, Rome was left without external military protection.

On September 20, 1870, after a brief symbolic resistance by the papal troops — about 13,000 men under General Hermann Kanzler, ordered by Pius IX to resist only enough to make clear that the occupation was an act of force and not a voluntary cession — the army of the newly proclaimed Kingdom of Italy, commanded by General Raffaele Cadorna, opened with artillery, after about three hours of bombardment, a breach of approximately 30 meters in the Roman wall near the Porta Pia, and occupied the city. September 20 is remembered as the day of the «Capture of Rome» (Presa di Roma), and the Porta Pia became one of the symbols of the Risorgimento.

A plebiscite organized by the new authorities on October 2 of that year formally ratified the annexation of Rome to the Kingdom of Italy — an overwhelming victory for the «yes» vote, also favored by the instruction of abstention given by the Roman Curia to Catholics. In 1871 the capital of the kingdom was moved from Florence to Rome. Pius IX, considering the occupation of his sovereign territory illegitimate, refused to recognize the new situation and to accept any agreement with the Italian government, including the so-called Law of Guarantees of May 13, 1871, which unilaterally offered the Holy See certain prerogatives of symbolic sovereignty and an annual financial compensation — refused by the pope because he considered it a gracious concession of the Italian State, and not a full recognition of his independence. Declaring himself a «prisoner of the Vatican», Pius IX began to live in voluntary seclusion within the walls of the Apostolic Palace, a stance of protest that his immediate successors — Leo XIII, Pius X, Benedict XV, and Pius XI — maintained for almost sixty years, refusing to leave the Vatican or to attend public ceremonies on Italian territory. This impasse between the papacy and the Italian State came to be called the «Roman Question».

The Roman Question was only resolved with the signing of the Lateran Treaties (or Pacts) on February 11, 1929, negotiated between Pope Pius XI, represented by the Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri, and the Fascist government of Benito Mussolini. The agreement, made up of a political treaty, a financial convention, and a concordat, formally recognized the full sovereignty and independence of the Holy See over a new and tiny Vatican City State — with about 44 hectares and a few hundred inhabitants, the smallest sovereign state in the world — definitively ending the former territorial extent of the Papal States in exchange for an international legal guarantee of papal independence, a financial indemnity for the loss of the territories in 1870, and the recognition of Catholicism as the state religion in Italy. The Pacts entered into force with the exchange of ratifications on June 7, 1929. Since then, the pope has ceased to be sovereign of a vast Italian territory, but has maintained full political autonomy over the small Vatican State, an arrangement later incorporated into the Constitution of the Italian Republic and revised by the Villa Madama agreement of 1984.

itens.resumo: Ecumenical council of 1869-1870 that defined the dogma of papal infallibility, interrupted by the invasion of Rome before it could complete its agenda.
itens.corpo:
Convoked by Pope Pius IX through the bull «Aeterni Patris» of June 29, 1868, the First Vatican Council opened solemnly in Saint Peter's Basilica on December 8, 1869, bringing together between seven hundred and more than seven hundred and fifty council fathers from every continent — a number and a geographical breadth unprecedented in the history of councils up to that time, a direct reflection of the Catholic missionary expansion of the nineteenth century. It was the first ecumenical council since Trent, three centuries earlier, and it took place at a time of strong tensions between the Catholic Church and the modern world: the advance of philosophical rationalism, of political liberalism, of unifying nationalism in Italy and Germany, and the growing secularization of European societies called into question, in the eyes of Pius IX and of a good part of the episcopate, the very foundations of traditional religious authority.

This concern had already been expressed by Pius IX in 1864, in the encyclical «Quanta Cura» and in the appended «Syllabus of Errors», which condemned eighty propositions of contemporary liberal, rationalist and socialist thought. The council was born, in large part, from the desire to give these concerns a solemn and organized doctrinal formulation. On April 24, 1870, the council fathers unanimously approved the dogmatic constitution «Dei Filius», on the Catholic faith, which affirmed the possibility of knowing the existence of God by natural reason and the impossibility of a true contradiction between faith and reason, both coming from the same divine source.

The document of greatest historical repercussion, however, came on July 18, 1870: the dogmatic constitution «Pastor Aeternus», on the Church of Christ, which defined two central and interconnected points — the primacy of universal jurisdiction of the bishop of Rome over the whole Church, and, in its final chapter, the dogma of papal infallibility. According to this definition, the pope enjoys infallibility, by special divine assistance, when he speaks «ex cathedra» — that is, when, exercising his office as supreme shepherd and teacher of all Christians, he solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church. The definition was approved by 533 votes in favor and only two against; a larger group of bishops who disagreed with the timeliness or the formulation of the doctrine — about 55, according to estimates — preferred to leave Rome before the final vote, rather than vote publicly against the wishes of the pope.

The vote on «Pastor Aeternus» coincided almost to the day with one of the most dramatic events of European politics of the century: on the day after its promulgation, July 19, 1870, the Franco-Prussian War broke out, which forced the withdrawal of the French garrison that had protected Rome for years. Without this military protection, the city became vulnerable to the advance of the troops of the Kingdom of Italy, who would occupy it in September of that same year, completing Italian unification at the expense of the last remnants of the Papal States. Faced with the impossibility of guaranteeing the freedom and security of the council's work in a Rome now under Italian sovereignty, Pius IX suspended the First Vatican Council indefinitely on October 20, 1870.

The council was never formally reopened nor closed by a conciliar act of its own, remaining, from the juridical-canonical point of view, merely suspended. Its original agenda — which still envisaged a complete schema on the nature of the Church as a whole, including the relationship between the pope and the bishops — remained pending for almost a century, revisited only with the convocation of the Second Vatican Council in 1962, whose constitution «Lumen Gentium» is seen by many theologians as the necessary complement that balances Vatican I's emphasis on the papal primacy with a broader ecclesiology of episcopal collegiality.
