itens.resumo: Ecumenical council of 1962-1965 that promoted a broad liturgical, ecclesiological and pastoral renewal of the Catholic Church in the contemporary world.
itens.corpo:
Elected in October 1958 at almost 77 years of age, and seen by many as a "transitional pope" who would leave no deep mark, John XXIII surprised the Catholic world by announcing, on January 25, 1959—less than three months after his election—the convocation of a new ecumenical council, the first since Vatican I, which was interrupted in 1870. The pope defined the aim of the council with a word that would become famous: "aggiornamento," updating—not a change in the doctrine of the faith, which John XXIII considered unchangeable, but a renewal of the language, the pastoral structures and the posture of the Church toward the contemporary world, so that the Christian message could be more effectively understood and lived.

After more than three years of preparation, with preparatory commissions that gathered thousands of suggestions ("vota") from the world episcopate, the Second Vatican Council was solemnly opened on October 11, 1962, in Saint Peter's Basilica, bringing together more than 2,400 bishops from every continent—the largest and most truly universal assembly in the history of councils, reflecting the maturity of the young Churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America. For the first time, the council also had the presence of official observers from other Christian confessions—Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans, among others—invited to follow the proceedings in a gesture of unprecedented ecumenical openness.

John XXIII would die on June 3, 1963, between the first and second of the council's four sessions, without seeing its end. His successor, Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini, elected a few weeks later with the name Paul VI, took on the task of leading the council to its conclusions, presiding over the three remaining sessions until its solemn closing on December 8, 1965. In all, the council promulgated sixteen documents—four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations—a body of teaching without precedent in any previous council.

Among the most influential texts is the constitution "Lumen Gentium," on the Church, which renewed the Church's self-understanding by presenting the Church first as the "People of God," before treating its hierarchical structure, and developed the doctrine of episcopal collegiality—the idea that the bishops, united with the pope, collectively share responsibility for the governance of the universal Church. The constitution "Sacrosanctum Concilium," approved as early as the first session in 1963, began the broad liturgical reform that replaced Latin with vernacular languages in most of the Mass and broadened the active participation of the faithful in worship—the most visible change, and the one immediately felt by ordinary Catholics throughout the world. The constitution "Dei Verbum" renewed the theology of Revelation and promoted the faithful's access to Sacred Scripture, and the lengthy pastoral constitution "Gaudium et Spes" dealt with the relationship between the Church and the contemporary world on themes such as culture, work, family, peace and economic development.

Other documents opened paths hitherto unexplored: the declaration "Nostra Aetate" established entirely new foundations for the Church's relationship with Judaism, Islam and the other non-Christian religions, explicitly repudiating every form of anti-Semitism; the decree "Unitatis Redintegratio" laid the foundations of the Catholic Church's modern ecumenical commitment to the other Christian confessions; and the declaration "Dignitatis Humanae" affirmed the right to religious freedom as a requirement of the dignity of the human person, going beyond more restrictive positions of earlier Catholic teaching on the relationship between Church and State.

Half a century after its close, the Second Vatican Council remains the most significant event in the recent history of the Catholic Church, but also one of the most debated: theologians, pastors and movements within the Church disagree about the extent to which its documents represent continuity or rupture with earlier Tradition, about the appropriate pace and extent of the liturgical reform that resulted from it, and about how to correctly apply, decades later, its vision of dialogue with the modern world—debates that have run through the pontificates of Paul VI, John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis, and that remain alive in the Church today.

itens.resumo: Armed conflict between 1926 and 1929, caused by the radical enforcement of anticlerical laws in post-revolutionary Mexico, which openly persecuted the Catholic Church.
itens.corpo:
The roots of the conflict go back to the Mexican Constitution of 1917, promulgated while the Mexican Revolution was still under way, which included strongly anticlerical articles: it denied legal personality to the churches, prohibited public worship outside church buildings, denied priests the right to vote and to engage in religious education, and subjected the number of authorized ministers of worship to state regulation in each State of the federation. During the following decade, these provisions were applied unevenly and often only nominally, until President Plutarco Elías Calles decided to enforce them with full rigor.

On June 14, 1926, Calles promulgated the so-called "Calles Law" ("Ley Calles"), which made a long list of religious activities a crime punishable by imprisonment and fines: wearing a religious habit in public, criticizing authorities or laws from the pulpit, and exercising the priesthood without state registration, among other restrictions. The Law took effect at the end of July of that year, and the Mexican episcopate, in direct protest against the new regulations, ordered the suspension of all public worship in churches throughout the country beginning on July 31, 1926 — an unprecedented measure of collective resistance that left millions of Mexican faithful without access to the sacraments.

The popular resistance, initially peaceful — through economic boycotts and petitions — turned into an armed uprising beginning in August 1926, above all in the rural States of west-central Mexico, such as Jalisco, Michoacán, Guanajuato and Zacatecas, where Catholic peasants, who called themselves "Cristeros" after their battle cry "Viva Cristo Rey!", organized militias that fought the federal army in a civil war of low intensity, but prolonged and bloody, that lasted until 1929. Historical estimates put the death toll at tens of thousands of combatants and civilians over the course of the conflict, with total estimates of victims — including displaced persons and indirect effects — reaching much higher numbers in some sources.

The persecution struck the clergy directly: priests were arrested, expelled from the country or summarily executed for continuing to celebrate Mass clandestinely. The best-known case is that of the Jesuit Miguel Agustín Pro, who worked clandestinely in Mexico City in disguise and under false identities in order to celebrate the sacraments, and who was arrested on the accusation — never proven — of involvement in an attack on a politician. Executed by firing squad on November 23, 1927 without a formal trial, he died with his arms outstretched in the form of a cross, refusing the blindfold and crying out "Viva Cristo Rey!" at the moment of execution — an event photographed and widely publicized by the Mexican government itself in an attempt to intimidate Catholic resistance, but which had the opposite effect, making him an immediate symbol of Cristero martyrdom. He was beatified by John Paul II in 1988.

The armed conflict only ended in June 1929, with a peace agreement mediated by the American ambassador Dwight Morrow between the government of President Emilio Portes Gil and the Mexican Catholic hierarchy, which restored public worship without formally repealing the anticlerical articles of the Constitution — a compromise solution that left latent tensions for decades, with sporadic outbreaks of anticlerical violence ("the second Cristiada") already in the 1930s. The episode left deep marks on Mexican culture and influenced literary works outside the country, among them the novel "The Power and the Glory" (1940), by the British writer Graham Greene, which portrays a fugitive priest during the Mexican religious persecution. Decades later, the Catholic Church would recognize the spiritual significance of that episode of resistance with the canonization of twenty-five Cristero martyrs by John Paul II in 2000.

itens.resumo: A period in which Western Christendom had two, and later three, rival popes at the same time, until the solution reached by the Council of Constance.
itens.corpo:
The Great Western Schism arose directly from the end of the Avignon Papacy: in 1377, Pope Gregory XI, yielding to appeals from figures such as Catherine of Siena, had finally returned the papal see to Rome after almost seven decades of French residence. His death in March 1378 obliged the cardinals — most of them French — to gather in conclave in a Rome filled with crowds loudly demanding an Italian pope, under the explicit threat of violence against the electors. Under this pressure, the conclave elected the Neapolitan archbishop Bartolomeo Prignano, who took the name Urban VI.

The new pope proved, within the first weeks of his pontificate, to be of an authoritarian temperament and aggressive toward the very cardinals who had elected him, to the point of humiliating them publicly. A few months later, in August 1378, a mostly French group of those same cardinals met separately and declared that the election of Urban VI had been invalid, since it had taken place under duress from the Roman crowd, and elected in his place Cardinal Robert of Geneva, who took the name Clement VII and settled in Avignon, resuming the old French seat, while Urban VI remained in Rome, refusing to resign. Thus began a double papal obedience that would divide Western Christendom for almost four decades.

Each of the two rival popes had successors, and the schism followed its own lines of succession: in Rome, Urban VI was followed by Boniface IX, Innocent VII and Gregory XII; in Avignon, Clement VII was succeeded by Benedict XIII. The recognition of each obedience followed above all the political alignments of the time, shaped in large part by the Hundred Years' War: France, Scotland, Naples, Aragon and Castile supported the Avignon line, while the Holy Roman Empire, England, Portugal and most of Italy and central Europe recognized the Roman line — a fracture that even reached religious orders and universities, internally divided according to the obedience of their members.

A first attempt at a solution, the Council of Pisa, convened in 1409 on the initiative of cardinals of both obediences weary of the impasse, was supposed to resolve the crisis by deposing the two rival popes and electing a third, Alexander V — but, since neither Gregory XII (Rome) nor Benedict XIII (Avignon) recognized his own deposition, the practical result was to worsen the situation, creating a third papal line and leaving Christendom divided among three simultaneous claimants to the throne of Peter, with Alexander V's successor, John XXIII, inheriting this third obedience.

The crisis was finally resolved only by the Council of Constance (1414-1418), convened under the protection of Emperor Sigismund. In the course of its proceedings, the council obtained the voluntary resignation of Gregory XII, formally deposed John XXIII and, unable to obtain the resignation of Benedict XIII — who would die still proclaiming himself the legitimate pope, isolated in a castle at Peñíscola, in Spain —, refused to recognize his authority. On November 11, 1417, the council elected by conclave a single pope recognized by all of Western Christendom: the Roman cardinal Oddone Colonna, who took the name Martin V, definitively ending the schism.

The episode dramatically exposed the fragility of the visible unity of the Church and had as a lasting theological by-product the strengthening of conciliarist currents, which — on the basis of the very decrees «Haec Sancta» and «Frequens» of the Council of Constance — held that the authority of an ecumenical council, representing the whole Church, was superior to that of any individual pope, including in matters of faith. This thesis, understandable as a reaction to decades of scandal and papal division, would generate theological tensions that the Church would resolve more clearly only centuries later, above all at the First Vatican Council (1870), by defining the primacy and infallibility of the pope in terms that definitively ruled out conciliar superiority over the Roman pontiff.

itens.resumo: A period of almost seventy years in which seven popes, all of them French, resided in Avignon instead of Rome, under strong influence from the French Crown, until Gregory XI's return to Rome in 1377.
itens.corpo:
The immediate background of the Avignon Papacy is the violent conflict between Pope Boniface VIII and King Philip IV the Fair of France at the beginning of the fourteenth century. In the bull «Unam Sanctam» (1302), Boniface had categorically asserted the submission of all temporal power to the spiritual authority of the papacy; Philip IV's response was to send agents who, in September 1303, in the episode known as the «Outrage of Anagni», seized and physically assaulted the elderly pope — an episode from which Boniface would never recover, dying a few weeks later. This outcome made it clear that the political power of the emerging national kingdoms already surpassed, in practice, the temporal authority of the medieval papacy.

After the brief pontificate of Benedict XI, the conclave of 1305, under strong influence from the French Crown, elected the Archbishop of Bordeaux, Bertrand de Got, who took the name Clement V — the first in a succession of seven French popes who would mark the following seventy years. Clement V never visited Rome after his election: crowned in Lyon, in the presence of Philip IV himself and his brother, he spent the first years of his pontificate moving through various French cities until he settled permanently, in 1309, in Avignon, a city on the banks of the Rhône that, although then part of the Holy Roman Empire (Kingdom of Arles) and not of the kingdom of France, lay directly within the orbit of French political influence. Under pressure from the French king, Clement V also presided over the process that led to the suppression of the Order of the Templars at the Council of Vienne (1311-1312), an episode widely seen by historians as a subordination of the papacy to the interests of the Crown.

Over the course of seven successive pontificates — Clement V (1305-1314), John XXII (1316-1334), Benedict XII (1334-1342), Clement VI (1342-1352), Innocent VI (1352-1362), Urban V (1362-1370) and Gregory XI (1370-1378), all of them French —, Avignon became established as the full papal seat. The imposing Palace of the Popes, one of the largest and most elaborate palace complexes of the late Gothic, was built in two main phases: the «Old Palace» (Palais Vieux), a sober fortress built by Benedict XII beginning in 1335 on the Rocher des Doms, and the more sumptuous «New Palace» (Palais Neuf), added by Clement VI. The curia became increasingly centralized and bureaucratized, with real administrative advances in the collection of ecclesiastical taxes, in banking organization and in canon law justice, factors that historians usually cite as a lasting administrative legacy.

Even so, geographical and political proximity to the French Crown compromised, in the eyes of a good part of Christendom — above all Italy, England and the Holy Roman Empire —, the spiritual independence of the Avignon popes: of the 134 cardinals created during this period, 111 were French, many of them relatives of the pontiffs themselves, a disproportion that fueled the suspicion that the Avignon papacy served, in practice, the interests of the kingdom of France. Under Clement VI, who had been Archbishop of Rouen and an adviser to Philip VI, this connection became even closer; modern historians, however, nuance this reading, observing that administrative centralization also answered to the Church's own purposes.

The period became known, already among contemporaries, by analogy with the biblical exile of the people of Israel in Babylon, as the «Babylonian captivity» of the Church — a term that the Italian poet and humanist Francesco Petrarch, a guest at the papal court in Avignon, himself helped to popularize in his criticisms of the luxury and corruption he saw in the Avignon curia. Influential voices, such as those of Saint Bridget of Sweden and above all Saint Catherine of Siena, pressed insistently for the return of the papacy to Rome, arguing that the See of Peter belonged by right and by tradition to the city of the apostles Peter and Paul.

The papacy would return definitively to Rome only when Gregory XI, responsive to these pressures and concerned about the deterioration of papal authority over the Papal States in Italy, left Avignon on September 13, 1376 and arrived in Rome on January 17, 1377, transferring the court back to the Eternal City. His death, a little more than a year later, in March 1378, would open the way for the even greater and longer-lasting crisis of the Great Western Schism, when Latin Christendom would find itself divided between rival papal obediences — one in Rome and another in Avignon — for almost forty years.

itens.resumo: Sixteenth ecumenical council, convened to end the Great Western Schism; it also tried and condemned the reformer Jan Hus.
itens.corpo:
Convened under the auspices of Emperor Sigismund of the Holy Roman Empire, the Council of Constance met in the imperial city in southern Germany from which it takes its name between November 5, 1414, and April 22, 1418, across forty-five general sessions — one of the largest and longest ecclesiastical assemblies of the entire Middle Ages, gathering at its height thousands of participants, including bishops, theologians, abbots, diplomats, and nobles from all over Europe. Its primary goal was to heal the Great Western Schism, which had divided Latin Christendom for thirty-six years among rival papal obediences, by then reduced to three simultaneous claimants: Gregory XII, recognized in Rome; Benedict XIII, in Avignon; and John XXIII, heir to the line elected by the failed Council of Pisa of 1409.

After complex negotiations, in 1415 the council obtained the voluntary resignation of Gregory XII — who, before resigning, formally convoked the council himself in order to legitimize its future acts, thereby preserving the juridical continuity of the Roman apostolic succession — and deposed John XXIII, who had tried to flee Constance in disguise but was captured and brought back for trial. Benedict XIII, isolated in his castle at Peñíscola, refused to appear or to resign, and the council simply declared his obedience extinct. Finally free of the three claimants, the council gathered in conclave and, on November 11, 1417, elected the Roman cardinal Oddone Colonna, who took the name Martin V, restoring a single papacy, recognized without contest throughout western Europe.

Alongside the resolution of the schism, the council set about trying the Bohemian theologian Jan Hus, rector of the University of Prague, whose ideas — strongly influenced by the Englishman John Wycliffe — criticized the wealth and corruption of the clergy, upheld the supreme authority of Scripture over ecclesiastical tradition, and went so far as to question the legitimacy of priests in grave sin exercising their ministry. Summoned to appear at Constance under a safe-conduct from Emperor Sigismund himself, which guaranteed him safety to go, present his defense, and return, Hus traveled voluntarily to the city in October 1414, confident that he could set out his positions before the assembly.

Despite the imperial guarantee, Hus was arrested a few weeks after his arrival, under pressure from the local clergy, who considered the safe-conduct invalid in matters of heresy — a legal principle that was already controversial then, and is still remembered today as a moral stain on the council. Held in prison for months, in poor sanitary conditions that worsened his health, Hus was finally tried, had his writings condemned as heretical, and, refusing to retract positions that he considered grounded in Scripture, was handed over to the secular arm. He was burned alive at the stake on July 6, 1415, maintaining, according to the accounts of the time, serenity in the face of death. The same council posthumously condemned the ideas of John Wycliffe, who had been dead for decades, ordering the exhumation and public burning of his remains — an order carried out only years later, in 1428.

The execution of Hus, seen in Bohemia as a betrayal of the imperial word and an attack on Czech national identity, provoked widespread revolt and set off the so-called Hussite Wars (1419-1434), a long and bloody conflict between the imperial and Catholic forces and the followers of Hus, who would become the basis of one of the first great pre-Protestant divisions of western Christendom — anticipating, more than a century earlier, central themes that the Protestant Reformation would take up with Luther. From the standpoint of Catholic ecclesiology, Constance also left an ambiguous and lasting legacy: its decrees «Haec Sancta» (1415), asserting the supreme authority of the council over any ecclesiastical authority, including the pope, and «Frequens» (1417), establishing the periodic and regular convocation of future general councils, fed for decades the conciliarist movement, which the Fifth Lateran Council, in the early sixteenth century, and later the First Vatican Council would explicitly seek to overcome.

itens.resumo: The third ecumenical council, convened by Emperor Theodosius II, which condemned Nestorianism and proclaimed Mary "Theotokos," Mother of God.
itens.corpo:
The controversy that led to the Council of Ephesus arose from the preaching of Nestorius, a Syrian monk trained in the theological school of Antioch and appointed Patriarch of Constantinople in 428 by Emperor Theodosius II. Concerned to preserve clearly the distinction between the human nature and the divine nature of Christ — a partly legitimate reaction against exaggerations that confused these natures — Nestorius began to publicly reject the traditional title "Theotokos" (Mother of God), attributed to Mary by popular devotion and by earlier authors, proposing in its place the term "Christotokos" (Mother of Christ), on the grounds that Mary had borne only the humanity of Jesus, not his eternal divinity.

Nestorius' position was seen by Cyril, the powerful and combative Patriarch of Alexandria, as a Christology that divided Christ into two distinct persons — one human, born of Mary, and the other divine, united to him only in a moral or functional way — contradicting the faith of the Church that in Christ there is only one person, the eternal Word, who assumed human nature in his incarnation. Cyril denounced Nestorius' position in doctrinal letters that would become classic Christological references, and as early as August 430 obtained a Roman synod, presided over by Pope Celestine I, which formally condemned the teachings of Nestorius and ordered his retraction under penalty of excommunication.

Faced with Nestorius' resistance, Emperor Theodosius II — initially favorable to him, but pressured by the intensity of the theological conflict that was dividing the East — convened a general council, which met in the Church of St. Mary in Ephesus beginning on June 22, 431. The course of the council was marked by serious procedural tensions: Cyril, presiding over the assembly by papal delegation, formally opened the sessions before the arrival of the group of Syrian bishops led by John of Antioch, who were coming to support Nestorius — a delay that the Antiochenes, on arriving days later, denounced as a deliberate maneuver to exclude them from the vote.

The bishops gathered under Cyril condemned the doctrine of Nestorius by a wide majority, deposed him from the patriarchate, and approved as an expression of the right faith Cyril's second letter to Nestorius, which would become a Christological reference text: since Christ is one person, the incarnate Word, it is legitimate and necessary — not mere popular piety, but a requirement of the faith itself — to call Mary the true Mother of God, since the one she bore according to the flesh is the eternal Son of God himself. In response, the Syrian bishops led by John of Antioch, who had arrived a few days later, met in a separate council and, in turn, deposed and excommunicated Cyril and the local bishop of Ephesus, Memnon — a procedural schism that would be healed only two years later.

It fell to Emperor Theodosius II, faced with the impasse of two rival councils meeting in the same city, to recognize as legitimate the assembly led by Cyril, a decision that Pope Celestine I confirmed in Rome. The reconciliation between Alexandria and Antioch came with the so-called Formula of Union of 433, negotiated directly between Cyril and John of Antioch, which affirmed simultaneously the unity of the person of Christ and the full integrity of his two natures — a formula that anticipated, almost twenty years earlier, the language that the Council of Chalcedon would definitively enshrine in 451.

Nestorius, deposed and finally exiled by imperial order to Upper Egypt in 435, would die decades later still maintaining, in his writings, that he had never taught the separation of Christ into two persons — a claim that modern theologians and historians view with greater sympathy than the polemic of the fifth century allowed. Communities of the East that remained faithful to the Antiochene Christology of the Nestorian tradition survived above all in Persia, beyond the direct reach of Roman imperial power, giving rise to the tradition now known as the Assyrian Church of the East, which preserves to this day a distinct ecclesial and liturgical lineage, with small communities also in India (the so-called Saint Thomas Christians of the Chaldean tradition).

itens.resumo: The fourth ecumenical council, convened by Emperor Marcian, which defined Christ as one person subsisting in two natures, human and divine.
itens.corpo:
The road to the Council of Chalcedon passed through a troubled episode, now known as the "Robber Council" (Latrocinium). In 448, the archimandrite Eutyches, superior of a monastery in Constantinople and a figure of great prestige at the imperial court, was accused of teaching that, after the Incarnation, Christ's human nature had been absorbed or dissolved by the divine nature, leaving him, in practice, with a single nature — a position that became known as Monophysitism. Condemned by a local synod presided over by Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople, Eutyches appealed to the powerful Patriarch of Alexandria, Dioscorus, successor of Cyril, who obtained from Emperor Theodosius II the convocation of a new general council at Ephesus in 449.

At this council — which posterity would reject and nickname the "Robber Council," an expression coined by Pope Leo the Great himself — Dioscorus presided over the proceedings in an authoritarian manner, refused to allow the reading of the doctrinal letter that Pope Leo the Great had sent on the matter (the "Tome of Leo," addressed to Flavian), rehabilitated Eutyches, and violently deposed Flavian, who would die a few days later as a result of the physical mistreatment he suffered during the session. Rome refused to recognize the decisions of that assembly, and only the death of Emperor Theodosius II, in a fall from a horse in 450, and the accession to the throne of Marcian and his wife Pulcheria made it possible to reverse the situation.

Marcian convened a new council, which met between October 8 and November 1, 451, in the city of Chalcedon, on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, opposite Constantinople — a place chosen for convenience and security, close enough to the capital to facilitate the imperial presence, but outside the direct influence of the court. The largest council of Christian Antiquity gathered there, with a number of participants that ancient sources estimate at between 500 and 600 bishops, the overwhelming majority from the Greek-speaking East; Pope Leo the Great, as was customary in this period, did not attend in person, but was represented by legates.

The council formally annulled the decisions of the "Robber Council," deposed and exiled Dioscorus of Alexandria, and received the "Tome of Leo" as an authentic expression of the faith; according to the traditional account, the bishops present greeted it with the acclamation "Peter has spoken through Leo." Relying on this text and on the earlier doctrinal letters of Cyril of Alexandria, the assembly formulated the so-called Definition of Chalcedon: in Christ, one person (one "hypostasis") subsists in two complete natures, divine and human, united "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation" — the four negative adverbs that would become the classic and definitive formula of all later orthodox Christology, both Catholic and Byzantine.

The reception of this formula, however, was far from unanimous. Important Churches of non-Greek tradition — in Egypt, most of the Coptic episcopate; in Syria and Armenia, a good part of the Syriac- and Armenian-speaking clergy; and later Ethiopia, ecclesiastically linked to Alexandria — refused to accept the Chalcedonian language of the "two natures," considering it excessively close to the Nestorianism already condemned at Ephesus, and preferring the Miaphysite formula of "one nature of the incarnate Word," an expression that Cyril of Alexandria had already used before Chalcedon and which these Churches understand, on theological interpretation, not to be properly Monophysite in the condemned sense. This refusal gave rise to the Chalcedonian schism, which still today separates the so-called Oriental Orthodox Churches — Coptic, Syriac Orthodox, Armenian, Ethiopian, and Eritrean — both from Rome and from the Byzantine Orthodox Churches of Greek and Slavic tradition, although theological dialogues in recent decades have significantly reduced, on both sides, the weight of these Christological divergences.

itens.resumo: Council convoked by Innocent III, with a record attendance of bishops, which defined the dogma of transubstantiation and the obligation of annual confession and Easter Communion.
itens.corpo:
No other medieval council reflected the personal strength of a single pope as directly as the Fourth Lateran Council reflected the pontificate of Innocent III, one of the most powerful and capable popes of the entire Middle Ages. Convoked by the bull «Vineam Domini Sabaoth» of April 19, 1213 — more than two years before it took place, an exceptionally long interval that allowed careful preparation —, the council assembled in the Basilica of Saint John Lateran, in Rome, throughout November 1215, with a single solemn public session on November 30. Attendance was unprecedented in medieval history up to that time: more than seventy patriarchs and archbishops, among them those of Constantinople and Jerusalem — under Crusader rule since the Fourth Crusade —, about four hundred bishops and nine hundred abbots and priors, representing practically all of Latin Christendom, as well as ambassadors from various European kingdoms.

The council's agenda was vast, and its seventy canons touched practically every aspect of the ecclesial and social life of the time. The first canon, doctrinal in character, set forth the Church's Trinitarian and Christological faith and, at a central moment in the history of sacramental theology, defined with the technical term «transubstantiation» — probably already in theological use for decades, but here officially enshrined for the first time in a conciliar document — that the bread and wine are changed, by divine power, into the substance of the body and blood of Christ during the Eucharistic consecration, even though their appearances (color, taste, form) remain unchanged. The same canon also affirmed, in a formula that would become classic, that «outside the Church there is absolutely no salvation» — an expression that later theology would interpret with increasing qualifications and nuances.

In the realm of everyday sacramental discipline, canon 21, known by its opening words «Omnis utriusque sexus» («Every faithful of either sex»), established for every Christian who had reached the age of reason the obligation to confess at least once a year to his own parish priest and to receive Communion at least at Easter, under penalty of exclusion from the Church during life and of Christian burial after death — a norm that profoundly and lastingly shaped Catholic sacramental practice, with echoes that persist in canon law to this day.

The council also dealt with questions of disciplinary reform of the clergy — the fight against simony, the requirement of minimal theological training, the regulation of priests' moral lives —, with norms on marriage and the degrees of kinship that impeded marriage (consanguinity), and with the preparation of a new expedition to the Holy Land, which would result in the Fifth Crusade. It also adopted canons that imposed restrictions and distinctive signs on Jews and Muslims living in Christian territories — provisions now recognized, including by the Church herself, as reflecting a deeply problematic medieval anti-Judaism that has been theologically superseded by the contemporary magisterium, especially since the Second Vatican Council.

In the doctrinal and disciplinary field, the council also formally condemned the Cathar (or Albigensian) and Waldensian heresies, then expanding rapidly in southern France and northern Italy, and expressly forbade the founding of new religious orders with their own original rule, distinct from those already existing — a provision that would oblige, for example, the Franciscans, then in formation, to formally adopt a rule recognized by the Holy See. The conciliar condemnation of Catharism also supplied the doctrinal justification that would sustain, in the following years, the military crusade waged against the Cathars of Languedoc, already under way since 1209 under the command of nobles from northern France.

itens.resumo: The longest and most violent Roman imperial persecution of Christians, begun by a series of edicts of Diocletian and brought to an end by the edict of toleration of Galerius.
itens.corpo:
After more than two decades of relative religious toleration since the end of the persecutions of Valerian in 260, the Roman Empire turned violently against the Christians once again under the rule of Diocletian (284-305), the emperor who had reorganized the Roman state into the so-called Tetrarchy — a system of shared government between two augusti and two caesars, of whom Diocletian was the senior. Historians attribute the initiative for the persecution above all to the influence of Galerius, caesar of the East and son-in-law of Diocletian, who was strongly hostile to Christianity and who is said to have convinced the older emperor, initially reluctant, to act after episodes interpreted as religious and political affronts — among them the refusal of Christian soldiers in the legions to take part in ritual sacrifices.

The persecution began formally on February 24, 303, with a first edict published in Nicomedia, the eastern capital of the Empire, which ordered the destruction of Christian churches, the seizure and public burning of the Scriptures, and the loss of civil and legal rights for Christians, who were barred, for example, from appealing to the courts. The first symbolic target of the edict was the cathedral of Nicomedia itself, demolished by imperial order the day after the edict was published. A second edict, still in 303, ordered the arrest of all the clergy — bishops, presbyters, and deacons — filling the imperial prisons to the point that the government itself had to release common criminals to make room for the imprisoned clergy.

A third edict, published on the occasion of the celebrations of the twentieth year of Diocletian's reign, offered amnesty to imprisoned clerics who agreed to offer public sacrifice to the Roman gods, a demand that many Christians, then already called «lapsi» when they yielded, accepted under torture or threat, giving rise to later internal debates about their reintegration into ecclesial communion. The fourth and harshest edict, published in 304, probably at the direct initiative of Galerius, extended the requirement of public sacrifice to all inhabitants of the Empire, lay Christians included, under penalty of torture and death — the most universal and systematic persecution the Church had faced until then.

The application of the edicts varied greatly according to the region and the local ruler: in the West, under the caesar Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine, the persecution was applied with considerable moderation, being limited in many places to the destruction of buildings without widespread physical violence against persons; in the East, under Diocletian and above all under Galerius and later Maximinus Daia, the persecution was relentless and prolonged, producing the most numerous and most dramatic accounts of martyrdom in all of Christian antiquity — among the most remembered victims are Saint Agnes of Rome, Saint Sebastian (whose martyrdom tradition places in this period), and the so-called Four Crowned Martyrs, in Pannonia.

After Diocletian's abdication in 305, the persecution continued unevenly under his successors, being most intense in the eastern regions controlled by Galerius and later by Maximinus Daia. The outcome came unexpectedly: in 311, already dying of a painful illness that the Christian chroniclers of the time, such as Lactantius, interpreted as divine punishment, Galerius himself — the chief instigator of the persecution — published on his deathbed an edict of toleration, acknowledging the failure of the campaign to eradicate Christianity and authorizing Christians to rebuild their places of worship and to profess their faith, in exchange for prayers for his health and for the prosperity of the state. This edict of Galerius, published two years before the better-known Edict of Milan of Constantine and Licinius (313), was the first official recognition, at the imperial level, of the definitive failure of the policy of persecuting Christianity in the Roman Empire.

itens.resumo: A document of Pope Boniface VIII, at the height of his conflict with King Philip IV of France, which asserted the subjection of all temporal power to papal authority.
itens.corpo:
The conflict between Pope Boniface VIII and King Philip IV the Fair of France began years before the bull that would become its greatest symbol, and arose from a concrete dispute: in 1296, Philip IV, needing funds to finance his war against England, decided to tax the French clergy without asking for papal authorization, violating traditional canonical practice. Boniface VIII reacted with the bull «Clericis Laicos», forbidding, under penalty of excommunication, any ruler to tax the clergy without the explicit consent of Rome. The dispute dragged on for years, aggravated by other episodes of friction, among them the king's imprisonment, in 1301, of the French bishop Bernard Saisset, on charges of treason — a direct attack, in the pope's eyes, on the traditional clerical immunity before secular justice.

These concrete conflicts over jurisdiction and taxation were part of a broader historical context: the growing assertion of the centralized power of the European national states, above all the French monarchy, in the face of the universal authority that the medieval papacy had claimed for centuries over all of Christendom. Philip IV surrounded himself with jurists trained in Roman law, such as William of Nogaret, who defended the full and exclusive sovereignty of the king over his kingdom, without papal interference in temporal matters — a view diametrically opposed to the hierocratic tradition that Boniface VIII, trained in canon law, sought to reaffirm in its full extent.

In response to the escalation of the conflict, Boniface VIII promulgated, on November 18, 1302, the bull «Unam Sanctam», one of the most categorical and theologically ambitious documents ever issued on the nature and extent of papal authority. The text begins by affirming the unity of the Church and its necessity for salvation, and develops the traditional image of the «two swords» — the spiritual and the temporal — to conclude that both belong, ultimately, to the Church: the temporal sword is to be wielded by kings and knights, but always in the service of the Church and under its guidance, while the spiritual sword is wielded directly by ecclesiastical authority. The bull culminates in its most quoted and most controversial sentence: that it is absolutely necessary for the salvation of every human creature to be subject to the Roman pontiff.

Philip IV's reaction was swift and violent. Convening the Estates General of the kingdom to obtain internal political support, the king sent his counselor William of Nogaret to Italy with instructions to confront the pope directly, who was then staying in his native city, Anagni, south of Rome. On September 7, 1303, allied with the Roman nobleman Sciarra Colonna — a member of a family that Boniface VIII had persecuted years earlier because of political rivalries internal to Rome —, Nogaret led a small army of several hundred soldiers that invaded the papal residence in Anagni, arrested and physically assaulted the pope, then almost 86 years old, even threatening him with death; according to some accounts, Colonna himself tried to slap him. The so-called «Outrage of Anagni» lasted about three days, until the local population, in revolt, expelled the invaders and freed the pope.

Boniface VIII never recovered physically and psychologically from the episode, dying in Rome a few weeks later, on October 11, 1303. The outrage of Anagni is today widely recognized by historiography as a symbolic landmark of the irreversible decline of the direct political power of the medieval papacy in the face of the growing strength of the European national states — a process that would have its immediate sequel a few years later, with the election of a French pope, Clement V, and the transfer of the papal seat to Avignon, under the direct orbit of the influence of the very French Crown that had humiliated Boniface VIII.

itens.titulo: The Great Jubilee of the Year 2000
itens.resumo: Extraordinary holy year proclaimed by John Paul II to celebrate the two thousandth anniversary of the birth of Christ, the only jubilee in which the pope himself opened the Holy Doors of the four papal basilicas of Rome, closed on January 6, 2001.
itens.corpo:
The preparation for the Great Jubilee of the Year 2000 began years before its celebration: as early as 1994, Pope John Paul II published the apostolic letter "Tertio Millennio Adveniente," calling the whole Church to a three-year period of preparation, each year dedicated to a person of the Trinity — the Son in 1997, the Holy Spirit in 1998 and the Father in 1999 — with special emphasis on reconciliation, the renewal of faith and the witness of divine mercy at the turn of the millennium. The tradition of jubilee years in the Catholic Church goes back to the year 1300, instituted by Pope Boniface VIII, and since then it has offered the faithful the possibility of obtaining plenary indulgences through pilgrimage, confession and other specific spiritual conditions. The jubilee of the year 2000 was formally proclaimed by the bull "Incarnationis Mysterium," of November 29, 1998, the first Sunday of Advent.

On Christmas Eve of 1999, wrapped in a colorful cope, Pope John Paul II knelt before the Holy Door of Saint Peter's Basilica, paused in prayer and solemnly opened it, officially beginning the Great Jubilee of the Year 2000, an extraordinary holy year proclaimed to celebrate the second millennium of the birth of Christ. According to the text of the bull of indiction itself, the opening of the Holy Door of Saint Peter's would precede "by a few hours" the inaugural celebration planned in Jerusalem and Bethlehem. It was the only jubilee in history in which the pope himself personally opened, on successive dates over the following days, the holy doors of the four papal basilicas of Rome — Saint Peter's (December 24, 1999), Saint John Lateran (December 25), Saint Mary Major (January 1, 2000) and Saint Paul Outside the Walls (January 18, the beginning of the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity) — a task that in earlier jubilees was normally delegated to cardinal legates.

During the 379 days it remained open, the Holy Door of Saint Peter's was a passage for more than twenty-five million pilgrims from all over the world, who could obtain the jubilee indulgence by visiting one of the patriarchal basilicas of Rome, participating in the Eucharist or devoting half a day to Eucharistic adoration; the same grace could be obtained in the Holy Land, by visiting the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, the Basilica of the Nativity in Bethlehem and the Basilica of the Annunciation in Nazareth, a gesture that underscored the universal, and not merely Roman, dimension of the jubilee celebration. In August 2000, at the heart of the holy year, Rome hosted the 15th World Youth Day, from August 15 to 20, with the theme "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us": about two million young people from 157 countries took part in the vigil and the Mass at Tor Vergata, presided over by John Paul II. The year was also marked by the "Martyrology of Christians who died in the twentieth century," an ecumenical memorial of the martyrs of the faith.

The jubilee year also included some of the most striking gestures of John Paul II's entire pontificate. On March 12, 2000, on the so-called "Day of Pardon," the pope presided in Saint Peter's Basilica over a penitential liturgy in which he publicly asked forgiveness for historical sins committed by children of the Church over the centuries — including religious violence, the Inquisition, divisions among Christians and sins against indigenous peoples, Jews and women —, an unprecedented historical examination of conscience in the papal tradition. Weeks later, from March 20 to 26, 2000, John Paul II made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, visiting Israel, the Palestinian territories and Jordan; on March 26, at what is known as the "Western Wall" (Wailing Wall) in Jerusalem, the pope paused in prayer and, following Jewish custom, placed in the crevices of the stones a handwritten note asking forgiveness for "the violence and crimes" committed against the Jews — an image that went around the world as a symbol of the pope's commitment to interreligious reconciliation.

The Great Jubilee came to a close with the solemn closing of the Holy Door of Saint Peter's on January 6, 2001, the feast of the Epiphany, with the singing of the hymn "Te Deum," ending a year that, according to the Holy See's own assessments, mobilized tens of millions of pilgrims between Rome and the Holy Land and is remembered as one of the moments of greatest public and spiritual visibility of John Paul II's entire pontificate, a few years before his death in 2005.

itens.titulo: The Black Death and the Church (14th Century)
itens.resumo: The pandemic that decimated Europe between 1347 and 1351 struck the clergy hard and gave rise to extreme religious movements, such as the flagellants, who were condemned by Pope Clement VI.
itens.corpo:
The Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347, probably carried by Genoese ships coming from Crimea along the trade routes of the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and spread with overwhelming speed across the continent over the following four years. It was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, transmitted by fleas living on rats — a mechanism of contagion that was then completely unknown, which made the disease all the more terrifying in the eyes of the medieval population. Mortality estimates vary, but historians calculate that between one third and one half of the European population died between 1347 and 1351, a demographic collapse without precedent in the continent's recorded history.

The epidemic struck the parish clergy with particular severity, since their pastoral duties — administering the last sacraments, hearing confessions, visiting and burying the dead — exposed them directly to contagion through close and repeated contact with the sick and the dying. Pope Clement VI, then residing in Avignon, wrote personally to a diocese that complained of an acute shortage of priests, citing a mortality rate among the clergy of about fifty percent in some regions — figures that, even if approximate, make clear how many parishes were left without priests for years, gravely compromising the sacramental life of entire communities precisely at the moment of greatest spiritual need.

The crisis deeply shook the religiosity of the age. With no medical explanation available, the plague was widely interpreted, by laity and by part of the clergy themselves, as divine punishment for the sins of Christendom, fueling practices of extreme penance and desperate searches for explanations and culprits. In this climate of collective panic, the flagellant movement resurged with unprecedented force — groups of laypeople, sometimes numbering in the thousands, who traveled through the cities and roads of central Europe publicly scourging their own bodies in penitential processions, in the belief that this self-mortification could appease the wrath of God and halt the advance of the plague.

The movement, at first tolerated or even viewed with sympathy by part of the hierarchy, became radicalized during 1349: the flagellants began to reject the sacramental mediation of the clergy and of the institutional Church, to preach apocalyptic prophecies about the imminent end of the world apart from any ecclesiastical authority, and, in tragic episodes recorded above all in Germany and the Low Countries, to instigate or directly take part in pogroms — violent massacres of Jewish communities, accused by baseless rumors of having poisoned wells and deliberately spread the plague. In the face of these excesses, Pope Clement VI took two notable measures: he formally condemned the flagellant movement by the bull «Inter Sollicitudines» in October 1349, ordering the bishops to suppress it; and, in earlier bulls of that same year, he explicitly defended the Jews against the accusations and popular violence, declaring that Christians who killed or expelled them without trial acted «seduced by that liar, the Devil», and ordering protection for the Jewish communities under penalty of excommunication for their attackers — a courageous position for the time, though of limited effectiveness given the violence already unleashed in several European cities.

Despite the papal condemnation of 1349, the flagellant movement resurfaced sporadically in later outbreaks of the plague throughout the 14th century, and was definitively suppressed only decades later, with a new explicit condemnation pronounced by the Council of Constance (1414-1418). The Black Death left lasting marks on European society and religious culture well beyond its acute phase: the shortage of trained clergy led to a general decline in the quality of priestly formation in the following decades, popular devotion turned with renewed intensity to saints who protect against plagues, such as Saint Roch and Saint Sebastian, and the profound shaking of confidence in institutions — ecclesiastical as well as medical and political — is now seen by many historians as one of the underlying factors that, alongside other crises of the 14th century, prepared the ground for the great religious and social transformations that Europe would experience in the following centuries.
